title: Security Issues and Solutions in Peer-to-Peer Systems for Realtime Communications
summary: Discusses security issues in peer-to-peer systems used for real-time communications such as VoIP, and describes possible solutions. It considers a world where traditionally centralized services run on peers. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: When phone calls rely on neighbors instead of one big company, you must trust strangers more. This document lists the dangers and ideas for staying safe.

questions: what are the security problems in p2p voip
how to secure peer-to-peer real-time communication
how to prevent poisoning attacks in p2p systems
subtitle: Security challenges when real-time communication relies on peers instead of centralized servers.

tldr.problem: When voice and video calls run on peer-to-peer systems instead of centralized servers, the trust model changes. Attackers can impersonate users, intercept calls, corrupt location data, and launch targeted attacks on individual peers, with higher stakes than in file-sharing networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC identifies attacker incentives, available resources, and victims, then describes defenses: admission control to vet new peers, reputation management to identify and isolate malicious nodes, redundancy to prevent censorship, iterative routing to detect poisoned responses, and end-to-end encryption to prevent eavesdropping.
tldr.outcome: These solutions highlight the research challenges of securing P2P systems used for personal communications. Some are incomplete (no perfect Sybil defense exists), and the field remains active.

facts.label: Core attacks discussed
facts.value: Sybil, denial of service, poisoning, eavesdropping

today: RFC 5765 is an Informational document published by the Internet Research Task Force. It represents the state of P2P security research as of 2010. No later updates or obsoleting RFCs exist. The security challenges described remain active research areas in the P2P and decentralized communication communities.

sections.title: Why Peer-to-Peer Real-Time Communication?
sections.content:
File-sharing networks like BitTorrent proved that P2P systems can scale without centralized servers. Real-time communication (VoIP, video chat) could gain similar benefits: fault tolerance, lower costs, and independence from any single provider. However, replacing centralized servers with a P2P overlay introduces new security risks.

P2P systems for calls and messaging are fundamentally different from file-sharing: users are unique (one per person), calls are private, and attacks on individual users have direct impact. A malicious file is a nuisance; a compromised call endpoint means loss of personal privacy.
sections.plainLanguage: A shared photo service can survive if someone posts a bad picture. A phone network cannot survive if calls are intercepted or hijacked.

sections.title: Who Attacks and Why
sections.content:
The RFC describes attacker profiles: those with financial motive (extortion, service disruption), those with ideological motive (copyright enforcement), and those with minimal resources (amateur hackers). Attackers with botnet access have substantial resources (bandwidth, IP addresses, computation). Without sufficient resources, defenses like cryptographic puzzles work; with botnets, they do not.

Attacks can target individual users (denial of service on their location in the overlay), content (poisoning or corrupting location records), or the entire network (overwhelming peers with false information). Attacks may begin immediately upon joining or after gaining trust.
sections.plainLanguage: A motivated attacker has many tools: fake machines, lots of internet bandwidth, or time to wait and learn the system. Defenses must work even against attackers with all three.

sections.title: Core Defense Strategies
sections.content:
Admission Control limits new peers. A prospective member proves compliance with a group charter and gets a certificate from a central or distributed authority. This raises a barrier against Sybil attacks (one person creating many fake identities), though a well-resourced attacker can create many certificates if the authority is fooled.

Reputation Management tracks peer behavior. Nodes assign trust or distrust vectors based on direct experience. Structured systems like EigenTrust propagate reputation through the network, but reputation can be gamed by collusion.

Redundancy (storing data at multiple nodes) defeats single-node censorship but requires careful node selection to prevent an attacker from controlling all replicas. Using diametrically opposite nodes in the ID space (far from each other) raises the cost for attackers.

Routing integrity prevents poisoned responses. Iterative routing (each hop verified) is slower but catches forgeries. Sending queries on multiple paths detects when responses differ.
sections.plainLanguage: Check who joins. Remember who misbehaves. Store copies of important data in multiple places, chosen so attackers would need many fake identities to control them all. Verify answers before trusting them.

sections.title: Challenges Specific to Real-Time Communication
sections.content:
Real-time systems use the same DHTs as file-sharing but store different data: user locations (who is online and where to reach them) instead of files. Location data is unique per user and attracts targeted attacks. A hijacked location allows call interception.

Peer promotion (converting client applications to peers contributing to the overlay) must be selective. Passive (invitation-based) promotion deters attackers who cannot predict when or if they will be invited. Active (self-service) promotion is simpler but allows brute force.

End-to-end encryption of media is essential but computationally expensive, especially on mobile devices. Signaling (call setup) is also vulnerable: if an attacker controls intermediate peers, they can fake call rejection or call transfer. Solutions include tunneling signaling through secure connections and using cryptographically-verified location bindings (hashing a public key to create a permanent user ID).
sections.plainLanguage: Phone calls must be private and reach the right person. Inviting only trustworthy devices to join the network makes attacks harder. Scrambling the call so only the other person can hear it stops eavesdropping.

sections.title: Open Problems
sections.content:
The RFC identifies five areas still unsolved: (1) assigning node IDs in a way that defeats Sybil attacks without a trusted authority, (2) binding identities to people (solving the problem of verifying who someone really is), (3) managing trust among peers without central authority, (4) resisting collusion by groups of malicious peers, and (5) recovering from attacks after they occur.

Most P2P systems in production (Skype, BitTorrent, content distribution networks) retain central components (login servers, trackers, moderators) to solve these problems. Pure P2P systems remain largely an open research question. The field continues to progress, but there is no consensus solution to the core challenges.
sections.plainLanguage: We still do not know how to stop one attacker from pretending to be thousands of people without a central authority. We still do not know how to bind a computer identity to a real person. Research is ongoing.
